newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo Jan-Aug money supply up 35 pct vs Dec - paper.
newsitem.headline: Yugo Jan-Aug money supply up 35 pct vs Dec - paper.

text.p: Yugoslavia's M1 money supply rose to over 4.4 billion dinars ($0.875 billion) at the end of August, rising 35 percent from December 1995 level, the Belgrade daily Nasa Borba reported on Thursday.
M1 money supply stood at 4.413 billion dinars on August 23, soaring 1.157 billion dinars over last December's level, the paper quoted a National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) report.
No-one at the NBY was immediately available for comment.
Month-on-month money supply growth ranged between 1.9 percent in January and 9.6 percent in April.
From mid year to August 23, M1 rose by another 10.3 percent, or 413 million dinars, the paper said.
According to the NBY report "the growth resulted primarily from higher hard currency sales, an increase in net forex reserves and more active bank lending to companies."
In the early months of the year, the share of cash in M1 money supply dropped to 39 percent from 44 percent in 1995.
Most bank credits went to the power industry and for financing agricultural production.
Total NBY placements on August 23 stood at 2.273 billion dinars, of which 1.763 billion was to banks, and 510.3 million to direct NBY customers.
Total retail banking sector long- and short-term placements stood at 8.109 billion at the end of June, in July 8.574 billion and in late August 9.075 billion dinars.
Bank liquidity was stable after NBY introduced harsh measures for commercial banks with negative balances.
Commercial banks had on average some 200 million dinars a day at their disposal until September 12, when the 10 percent reserve requirement imposed by the central bank came into effect.
While disposable amounts in the banking sector stood at 190.6 million dinars on September 5, ten days later this amount melted down to 109.5 million.

At the same time, the reserve requirement filled NBY coffers. The reserve requirement special account recorded a dramatic surge from 15.5 million on September 9 to 231.8 million on September 12. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
